fact_check_log.claim: Getting married in Brazil legally means the civil process at a Cartório de Registro Civil, the civil registry office. You apply to be cleared to marry, a step called the habilitação, at the civil registry of the district
Brazilian law clears couples to marry through a habilitação at a civil registry office, after which they can marry before any registry office of their choice while the clearance is valid.
Foreign documents generally need an apostille at home and then a sworn Portuguese translation that can only be done in Brazil, so build time in Brazil for it.
A religious ceremony can carry civil effect when the couple are cleared first and the marriage is registered within 30 days of the ceremony.

For Australians, a Certificate of No Impediment comes from DFAT or the Australian Embassy in Brasília, and an overseas marriage is in most cases recognised at home if it was valid where it took place.

The legal route is the civil process. Brazil's Public Registries Law sets out how it works, as at November 2026: you present the documents the civil law requires and ask the civil registrar of the district where one of y
The habilitação is your application to marry. You bring the documents the civil law asks for, and the registrar checks them.
Identification and the documents can be presented electronically, with proof that they are authentic and unaltered.
If the documents are in order, the registrar publishes your application electronically and issues the certificate of habilitação within up to 5 days.
With that certificate, you can marry before any civil registry office you choose, within the validity period the Civil Code sets.
If anyone raises an impediment or objection, the registrar tells you, the matter goes to a judge with the Public Prosecutor's office informed, and the judge decides.

The public notice of your intention to marry is called the proclamas, the banns. The electronic publication can be dispensed with in cases the law provides for, if you petition the registrar with proof of urgency, and th
As a general rule, documents issued abroad must be legalised and translated before Brazilian authorities accept them.

The apostille is the faster form of legalisation: under the Hague Apostille Convention, in force in Brazil since 2016, documents from member countries are accepted with a single apostille, with no separate consular step.
An apostille is a certificate that authenticates the origin of a public document.
In Brazil, foreign documents, even when apostilled, must be translated by a tradutor juramentado, a sworn public translator, to be valid, and that translation can only be done in Brazil.
For Australians: a Certificate of No Impediment to Marriage, or CNI, is a DFAT document that proves you are not already married, for when local authorities ask.
At least one of you must be an Australian citizen or permanent resident, and DFAT issues CNIs through Australian Passport Offices, through embassies and consulates overseas, and by mail.
A fee applies, paid when you apply.

DFAT does not advise on another country's legal process. Ask the cartório whether it needs a CNI at all, whether it accepts a Single Status Certificate or No Record Result Certificate from your state or territory registr
Local authorities may also ask for divorce papers, a deceased spouse's death certificate, your original birth certificate and your passport.
The CNI form is signed in front of an authorised witness, such as a Justice of the Peace or Australian Passports official at home or a consular official overseas.

In Brazil, the [Australian Embassy in Brasília](https://brazil.embassy.gov.au/) and the Consulate-General in São Paulo provide notarial services, including CNIs and apostilles, by appointment only, and fees apply.
Embassy staff will not say which documents you need, and a CNI application mailed from within Brazil is accepted only if a local notary at a cartório witnessed the signature.
The Honorary Consulate in Rio de Janeiro does not provide notarial services.
The marriage record is signed by the person presiding, the two of you, your witnesses and the registrar, and there must be at least two witnesses unless the law provides otherwise.
Once the certificate of habilitação is issued, the civil marriage is celebrated on the day, at the time and in the place you request and the registrar sets.
Ask the cartório who will conduct your ceremony, because the person presiding signs your marriage record with you.
Straight after the ceremony, a record is drawn up and signed. It notes your details, the date of the banns and of the ceremony, the documents you presented and your marriage property regime.
Ask the cartório to explain the property regime options before the day, so you choose rather than default. Its registration takes legal effect from the ceremony date.
You can ask the registrar for the certificate of habilitação so that you can marry before a religious authority or minister, and it states how long the clearance is valid.
The record of a religious marriage is signed by the celebrant, the two of you and two witnesses.

Within 30 days of the religious ceremony, the celebrant or anyone with an interest can ask the registry office that issued the certificate to register the marriage, and the registrar registers it within 24 hours.
Registration takes legal effect from the date of the ceremony.
The place of the civil ceremony is one you request and the registrar sets.
You can also marry at any civil registry office of your choice while your clearance is valid, and hold the celebration separately.

For Australians: you cannot register an overseas marriage in Australia, but in most cases it is legally recognised if it was valid under the law of the country where it took place and would have been valid under Australi
Australia does not recognise an overseas marriage where either person is already married, not old enough to marry, too closely related, or forced to marry.

A foreign marriage certificate is usually accepted as proof of the marriage, but it may not work as proof of a name change, so check with your state or territory registry of births, deaths and marriages.
Smartraveller suggests talking to a lawyer to confirm your certificate is valid in Australia.
In Brazil, apostilles on public documents are issued by authorised cartórios, which the National Council of Justice lists by state and city.
Once Australia recognises your marriage, you cannot marry again in Australia, though you may hold another kind of ceremony, such as a confirmation of vows.

For Australians: you need a visa to enter Brazil and must arrange it before arrival; it cannot be obtained at the airport, and travellers who arrive without one are sent back on the next available flight.
Entry and exit conditions can change at short notice, so check with a Brazilian embassy or consulate.
Passports are stamped on arrival and may be inspected on departure.
Dual nationals must enter and leave Brazil on their Brazilian passport.
You may need a valid yellow fever vaccination certificate to enter Brazil, and some airlines may ask for a copy when you depart.
Smartraveller advises Australians to "Exercise a high degree of caution" in Brazil due to the threat of violent crime.

It says violent crime including mugging, armed robbery and carjacking is common, more often in large cities and during festivals such as Carnival, and advises against going out alone at night and against isolated areas,
It advises using only prepaid or official taxis or app rideshare, matching the plate and driver name.
Drink spiking is a risk, so drink only branded, sealed drinks.
Brazil's wet season depends on where you are: January to July in the north, November to March in the south and south-east, and April to July in the north-east, and heavy rain can occur all year.
Landslides and flooding occur, and severe storms often delay flights.
Wildfires are common from May to September, especially in July and August.
Domestic and international flight delays are common.
On the paperwork side, a fee applies for an Australian CNI and for the Embassy's notarial services.
A fee also applies for legalising Australian documents through DFAT.
Your guests will need travel insurance, because Smartraveller says private health care in larger cities is very expensive and that cover must include all medical costs, including evacuation.
Visit Brasil, the national tourism board, lists Rio de Janeiro, Trancoso, Paraty, Florianópolis, Fernando de Noronha, Salvador, Búzios and Praia do Forte among its sun and beach destinations.
Rio de Janeiro sits in the south-east, where the wet season runs from November to March.
Many beaches, including in Rio de Janeiro, have strong rips.
Smartraveller names Copacabana Beach, Ipanema Beach, the Pedra do Sal area, Santa Teresa, Lapa, the Christ the Redeemer statue and the Corcovado Trail as crime hotspots.
If you picture photographs at a landmark, ask your photographer and venue how they plan timing and transport. English-speaking Tourist Police operate in Rio de Janeiro.
Paraty is on the Visit Brasil list alongside Búzios.
Trancoso, Salvador and Praia do Forte are on the same list.
In the north-east the wet season runs from April to July.
Shark attacks are possible at north-eastern beaches such as Recife, so ask your venue where guests can swim.
Florianópolis in the south and the island of Fernando de Noronha complete the list.
